profile.reading: This Data4 facility, coded MAD02, is located in San Agustin del Guadalix, 28750 Madrid, Spain, part of the operator own 2 building Madrid campus. The operator own page gives this building a capacity of 50 MW across approximately 6.7 hectares. The full Madrid campus totals 10.7 hectares and 100 MW combined across both buildings, MAD01 and MAD02. Data4 is a data center operator founded in 2006 and headquartered in Paris, France, operating campuses in France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Germany, and Greece. Data4 was founded in 2006 and is headquartered in Paris, France, described in the company own 2019-era published materials as controlled by AXA, the French insurance and asset-management group. Data4 own site describes a six-country European footprint spanning France, Italy, Spain, Poland, Germany, and Greece, totaling roughly ten campuses, 1.5 gigawatts of capacity, and 165,000 square meters of IT space group-wide. This record marks the broader MAD2 campus area at San Agustín del Guadalix, distinct from the two individual numbered buildings, MAD2-DC01 and MAD2-DC02, mapped separately elsewhere in this dataset. San Agustín del Guadalix sits north of Madrid, a newer data center growth corridor for the metro area as the more established Alcobendas site nearby has filled in with Data4 own MAD1 campus. Data4 has operated in Spain since expanding beyond its French home market, and Madrid two-site presence, MAD1 in Alcobendas and this newer MAD2 site in San Agustín del Guadalix, reflects a broader pattern across Data4 European portfolio of pairing an established first campus with a second, larger-capacity site once local demand justifies the additional investment, a pattern also seen in Data4 Milan market documented elsewhere in this dataset under the Data4 Italia operator name. No tenant is named.

reading.body:
Data4's Madrid MAD2 facility holds 50 MW of capacity across 6.7 hectares, part of a 100 MW, two-building campus that anchors European data center supply outside the US and major Asian hubs.

Data4 operates across six European countries from Paris, positioning itself as infrastructure for compute demand that cannot reach saturation in traditional American and Asian data center clusters. The Madrid campus alone, at 100 MW combined across both buildings, represents substantial scale for a single metro area. Yet this facility publishes zero megawatts currently deployed, indicating either planned capacity not yet activated or data lag in available sourcing.

The absence of power consumption data leaves a critical gap. Whether MAD2 operates at full capacity, partial capacity, or remains under deployment cannot be determined from available sources. For tracking AI's binding constraint, the difference between 50 MW nameplate and actual draw is material. Spain's power grid and the facility's connection to it are not described here, nor is the source of its electricity or any purchase agreements.

Data4's European footprint matters for AI scaling only if these campuses can absorb demand that US and Asia-Pacific operators cannot meet. The data confirms the buildings exist and their headline capacity. It does not show whether they are full, whether power is available to fill them, or whether they serve AI workloads specifically.
